questions.prompt: A describing function replaces a nonlinearity, for a sinusoidal input of amplitude \(a\), by
questions.explanation: The describing function keeps the fundamental and discards the harmonics. It is a gain, often real, and for a saturation or a relay it falls as \(a\) grows. It is not exact, because the harmonics are real. A gain with no amplitude dependence is the linear case. The DC gain misses the fundamental of an odd nonlinearity, which has no DC term.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls as amplitude grows.
options: one complex gain for the fundamental harmonic, which may depend on \(a\)
the exact response, including every higher harmonic
a linear gain that does not depend on amplitude
the DC gain of the nonlinearity

questions.prompt: An ideal relay switches between \(-3\) and \(+3\). For a sinusoidal error of amplitude 1.5, its describing function \(N(a) = 4M/(\pi a)\) equals
questions.explanation: \(N = 4\cdot 3/(\pi\cdot 1.5) = 2.54648\). Using \(M/a = 2\) drops the Fourier factor \(4/\pi\). Using \(4M/\pi\) and forgetting to divide by \(a\) leaves the fundamental coefficient, not the gain.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls as amplitude grows.

questions.prompt: That relay describing function is real and positive. The point \(-1/N\) on the real axis is
questions.explanation: Limit-cycle balance is \(G(j\omega) = -1/N\). With \(N = 2.54648\), the point is -0.392699. Plotting \(-N\) puts the critical point on the wrong side of \(-1\) and far too far left. Plotting \(-a\) uses the amplitude instead of the gain.

questions.prompt: An ideal relay of level \(M = 2\) has describing function \(4M/(\pi a)\). The amplitude \(a\) that makes \(N(a) = 2\) is
questions.explanation: \(8/(\pi a) = 2\) gives \(a = 4/\pi = 1.27324\). Solving \(4M/(\pi N)\) with the numbers swapped, \(a = 2\pi/4\), inverts the role of \(N\). The level \(M = 2\) is not the amplitude.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls as amplitude grows.

questions.prompt: A predicted limit cycle of a relay feedback loop is the intersection of
questions.explanation: The harmonic-balance condition is \(G(j\omega) N(a) = -1\), so \(G(j\omega)\) meets \(-1/N(a)\). The origin is the high-frequency end of many Nyquist plots, not the balance point. Step-response limits are a time-domain picture. The root locus does not carry the amplitude parameter \(a\).

the Nyquist plot of the linear plant with the locus \(-1/N(a)\)
the step response with the saturation limits
the root locus with the imaginary axis, for every amplitude

questions.prompt: A unit-slope saturation clips at \(\pm 1\). The input amplitude is 2, so the linear region covers only half of the sine wave. The describing function is
questions.explanation: With \(\delta = M/(k a) = 1/2\), \(N = (2/\pi)(\sin^{-1}\delta + \delta\sqrt{1-\delta^2}) = 0.608998\). The unsaturated gain would stay 1, which is the answer only for amplitudes below the clip. The relay formula \(4/(\pi a)\) is a different nonlinearity.
questions.figure_alt: A gain that falls once the amplitude exceeds the clip.

questions.prompt: The describing-function approximation is most believable when
questions.explanation: The method assumes the input of the nonlinearity is nearly sinusoidal. A low-pass plant attenuates the harmonics before they come around the loop. A plant that amplifies the third harmonic breaks that assumption. With no plant there is no loop to balance. Instability of every linear gain is a different question.

the nonlinearity is the only block and there is no plant

questions.prompt: An ideal relay of level 5 and a sine of amplitude 4 have describing function
questions.explanation: \(N = 4\cdot 5/(\pi\cdot 4) = 5/\pi = 1.59155\). The ratio \(M/a = 1.25\) omits \(4/\pi\). The product \(M a = 20\) is not a gain.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls as amplitude grows.

questions.prompt: A relay of level \(M = 1\) is in feedback with a linear plant. The balance \(N(a) = 2\) occurs at amplitude
questions.explanation: \(4\cdot 1/(\pi a) = 2\) so \(a = 2/\pi = 0.63662\). Using \(a = N\) gives 2, which sets the amplitude equal to the gain. Using \(a = 4M/\pi\) forgets to divide by the required \(N\).

questions.prompt: A linear block has peak gain 1.8. The small-gain idea says the loop stays stable for every stable perturbation whose gain is below
questions.explanation: The product of the two gains has to stay below 1, so the perturbation gain must stay below \(1/1.8 = 0.555556\). The peak gain 1.8 itself is already larger than 1 and is not a sufficient bound on the perturbation. Half of 1.8 is a guess, not the reciprocal.

questions.prompt: An odd, memoryless nonlinearity such as an ideal relay or a saturation has a describing function that is
questions.explanation: Odd memoryless maps produce a fundamental that is in phase with the sine, so \(N(a)\) is real. A relay with hysteresis is the case that adds a phase lag, because it has memory. A differentiator's \(+90^\circ\) is a linear phase, not a describing function. \(N(a)\) is zero only in the trivial case of no output.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls as amplitude grows.
options: complex, with a lag that grows with amplitude

questions.prompt: The Fourier series of an ideal relay (a square wave) has a third harmonic whose amplitude is what fraction of the fundamental?
questions.explanation: The square-wave coefficients fall as \(1/n\) for odd \(n\). The third harmonic is \(1/3\) of the fundamental, so the fraction is 0.333333. A fraction of \(1/9\) would be the square of that decay, which is not how the series works. A fraction of 1 would say the harmonic is as large as the fundamental, which is the case the describing function refuses.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls as amplitude grows.
